newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission moves to guarantee access to TV sports.
newsitem.headline: Commission moves to guarantee access to TV sports.

text.p: The European Commission moved on Wednesday to ensure that European sports fans can continue to watch live television coverage of major events without having to pay.

The Commission proposed an amendment to the TV without frontiers directive, 89/552/EEC, to allow national governments to guarantee viewers free access to coverage of events such as the Olympic Games, World Cup soccer finals and Tour de France cycle race.
Pay TV operators that won exclusive rights to broadcast those events would have to ensure they were offered unscrambled or on a non-subscription channel.

The proposal is in the form of the Commission's negotiating position in a European Parliament-Council of Ministers conciliation procedure on the proposal, COM(95)86, to amend the TV without frontiers directive.
Audiovisual Commissioner Marcelino Oreja told a news conference the proposal struck a balance between the public interest and the right of sports federations and pay-TV channels to earn money.
Based on the principle of "mutual recognition" of national lists, it is a more flexible approach than the one proposed by the parliament, which advocated a mandatory EU-wide list of "free" events.

It was welcomed by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which represents public broadcasters, but criticised by the Association of Commercial Television in Europe (ACT), whose members include pay-TV operators BSkyB, Canal Plus and Premiere.
The initiative reflects growing concern, especially in the parliament, about expensive bidding wars for television rights to major sports events involving pay-TV operators.
Last July, for example, Germany's Kirch group paid $2.2 billion to win the battle for TV rights to the 2002 and 2006 World Cup soccer finals.
That deal represented a "quantum leap" in payments for exclusive sports rights, the Commission said in its proposal.

"Our main concern is that all the major sports events would slowly but surely become pay TV events, which would deprive a large amount of the population from viewing them," an EBU official who asked not to be named told Reuters.

But ACT argues that sports organisations should have the right to dispose of TV rights as they see fit. "Organisers of sports events carry a considerable risk in today's economic environment, where top sport is dependent on heavy financing from television revenue," it said in a statement.

The Commission proposed a system under which countries may draw up lists of events that are of "major importance for society" either EU-wide, nationally or even regionally -- for example, the Scottish FA Cup soccer Final, the Commission said.
Those must be recognised by broadcasters from other EU countries. The events would have to meet certain criteria, for example they could not be matches that take place frequently.

For events of national or regional importance, the member state would be required to consult all interested parties and then notify draft measures to the Commission. The Commission would decide whether to approve the list after consulting a committee of national experts.

Britain, France and Belgium already have such lists. Britain includes the Wimbledon Tennis Championships, for example, and France the Tour de France, while Belgium's Flemish community draws up a list every year.

The proposal would not affect procedures for purchasing exclusive rights. Commission officials said broadcasters would still profit from advertising and sponsorship and would be able to sell the rights to television channels in the countries concerned.

The Commission noted in its proposal that EU action was warranted since eight member states had already enacted measures restricting the acquisition or exercise of exclusive broadcasting rights for major events, while three more were considering action.

"This uncoordinated development of national legal measures may be attributed, in part, to the fact that this field is not among those coordinated by the (television without frontiers) directive," it said.
